AFFILIATE DISCLOSURE CHECKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your affiliate disclosure missing, or just too late?

Paste a blog post or page's HTML and see every affiliate link it recognises — an Amazon Associates tag= link, an amzn.to short link, rel="sponsored", or a known network's tracking link (ShareASale, CJ, Impact, Skimlinks, AWIN, and similar) — and whether a disclosure phrase appears before the first one, the way the FTC's Endorsement Guides call for. Separately, it checks whether any Amazon link carries Amazon's own required exact statement — a generic "affiliate links" note is not enough for Amazon specifically, and Amazon has terminated associate accounts over exactly this gap.

Nothing is uploaded. The text box is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device. This is a fact-check, not a compliance determination: it names what it found, not whether you are safe from the FTC or from Amazon.

1. Paste your page's HTML

2. What was found

Affiliate link foundWhy it's flagged
Disclosure phrase foundKind

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a pre-publish gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — and it can walk a whole built site (e.g. a static blog's output directory) in one pass:

node cli.mjs check post.html                     # one file, human-readable
node cli.mjs check dist --json                      # a whole build output dir, machine-readable
node cli.mjs check dist --strict                    # also fail on a missing Amazon-required phrase

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only the local files/directories you name: no network call, ever. Exits 1 if any file is missing a disclosure, or discloses only after the first affiliate link.

What's checked

SignalWhat it means
Amazon Associates tag= link, or amzn.toAmazon's own tracking parameter / link shortener
rel="sponsored"Google's own recommended annotation for a paid or affiliate link, any network
Known affiliate-network tracking domainShareASale, CJ/Commission Junction, Rakuten/LinkSynergy, Impact, Skimlinks, VigLink, rewardStyle/LTK, AWIN, AvantLink, and similar
Generic tracking parameterirclickid=, affiliate_id=, aff_id=

Matched against visible text and link markup only — <script>, <style>, and HTML comments are never scanned. It cannot see a link built dynamically by client-side JavaScript that never appears in the pasted markup, and it does not attempt to identify every affiliate network in existence — only the widely-used ones listed above.

More: what disclosure Amazon Associates and the FTC actually require, and where to put it. Never written a disclosure yet? See this checker vs. Post Affiliate Pro's Disclosure Generator. Already have one and just want to know if it's placed right? See this checker vs. checking a post by eye.

Common questions

Why does this matter for Amazon Associates specifically?

Amazon's Associates Program Operating Agreement requires every page carrying an Associates link to state, in substance, "As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases." Amazon has terminated associate accounts for missing this, which removes the account's entire earning history, not just future commissions — so a missing disclosure is a real, checkable income risk, not a hypothetical one.

Is a generic "affiliate links" disclosure enough for an Amazon link?

Not for Amazon specifically. The FTC's Endorsement Guides ask for a clear and conspicuous disclosure in general, which a generic phrase like "this post contains affiliate links" can satisfy — but Amazon's own operating agreement additionally requires its specific exact statement, so this tool checks the two separately and flags an Amazon link that has some disclosure but not Amazon's own required wording.

Does this tell me whether I am FTC or Amazon compliant?

No. It reports which affiliate-link signals and which disclosure phrases it found, and their order on the page — facts about the text, not a legal or contractual determination. Read the FTC's Endorsement Guides and Amazon's own Associates Program Operating Agreement, and consult a professional if you need a determination you can rely on.

Is my content uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the HTML you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only local files — no network call, ever.

vs-checking-a-post-by-eye.html.text:
← Affiliate Disclosure Checker

Affiliate Disclosure Checker vs. checking a post by eye

Re-reading a post you already published catches an obviously missing disclosure. It reliably misses an affiliate link hidden behind ordinary anchor text, a rel="sponsored" attribute with no visible marker at all, and whether the disclosure actually sits before the first affiliate link once a post has more than one — which is what this free, no-upload checker computes exactly, in one pass.

Where re-reading it yourself stops being enough

Every blogger who has ever added an affiliate link already does this: publish the post, then read it back and check whether the disclosure is there. For the obvious case — no disclosure sentence anywhere on the page — that read-back is enough on its own. The problem is the other three things a real disclosure check needs are not visible from reading the rendered words at all.

What you're trying to confirmReading the post yourselfThis checker
No disclosure sentence anywhere on the page.Works. This is the one case a plain read-back reliably catches.Also catches it, in the same pass as everything below.
An affiliate link disguised behind ordinary anchor text ("click here", "this gadget") — the tracking signal is in the href, not the words you read.Invisible while skimming rendered text. Confirming it means opening view-source and checking every link's underlying URL by hand, one at a time.Classified automatically from the href against known Amazon, ShareASale, CJ, Impact, Skimlinks, AWIN, and similar tracking patterns.
A rel="sponsored" attribute with no visible marker on the page at all.Cannot be seen by reading the page; it exists only in markup a reader never renders.Read directly from the anchor's rel attribute.
Whether the disclosure genuinely appears before the first affiliate link, once a post has several links spread across multiple paragraphs.Requires holding your reading position and every link's position in mind at once and comparing them — easy to misjudge in a longer post.Computed as an exact character-offset comparison between the disclosure and every recognised link.
Whether an Amazon link specifically carries Amazon's own required exact statement, as distinct from a generic "affiliate links" note.Easy to assume a generic disclosure covers it — both read as disclosure-shaped sentences.Checked as a separate condition from the generic disclosure match.
Re-checking an entire blog's back catalogue after adding a new affiliate link somewhere.One post at a time, remembered by hand, every time something changes.One CLI command against a whole build-output directory.

A quick read-back is still the fastest way to catch a post with no disclosure at all, and this checker is not doing anything a careful line-by-line audit couldn't — it is reading the same markup a careful audit would, just checking every link's href and every character position automatically instead of leaving the comparison to be remembered by hand.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: the browser page parses HTML you paste entirely in your own browser, and the CLI reads only local files. Neither ever sends your content anywhere.

Common questions

Can't I just re-read my post and check for the disclosure myself?

For a post with one affiliate link and a disclosure sentence right above it, yes -- that case is obvious on a single read. What re-reading does not reliably catch is a disclosure that is present but appears after the first affiliate link rather than before it, an affiliate link whose href carries a tracking domain or parameter you did not recognise while skimming the rendered text, or a rel="sponsored" attribute that has no visible marker at all. Those need the actual markup checked in the order a reader encounters it, not remembered while reading the words.

Why is spotting an affiliate link harder than it looks?

Because the signal that makes a link an affiliate link lives in the href, not in the anchor text you actually read. "Buy it here" gives no clue whether the underlying URL carries an Amazon tag= parameter, routes through a shortener like amzn.to, or goes through a tracking domain such as shareasale.com, cj.com, impact.com, or skimlinks.com -- and rel="sponsored" is an attribute on the tag, never rendered as visible text at all. Confirming any of that means opening view-source and checking every link's markup by hand, one link at a time, which is exactly the comparison a skim of the rendered page does not do.

Doesn't having a disclosure somewhere on the page cover it?

No -- the FTC's guidance is specifically about a disclosure appearing before the first affiliate link a reader would encounter, not merely existing on the page. In a short post with one link near the top, eyeballing that order is easy. In a longer post with several affiliate links scattered across multiple paragraphs, correctly judging whether your disclosure sentence's position precedes every one of them means holding both positions in mind at once and comparing them -- which is a character-by-character ordering question, not a skim.

Is a generic "affiliate links" note enough for an Amazon link?

Not for Amazon specifically, and this is the mistake reading a post yourself is most likely to miss: a generic disclosure phrase reads as sufficient at a glance, so nothing about re-reading a post prompts you to check for Amazon's separate, exact required wording ("As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases"). The two are easy to conflate on sight because both are disclosure-shaped sentences; only checking for the exact phrase, not just the presence of some phrase, tells them apart.

Is this page making a live comparison against a tool or company?

No. This page describes a manual habit every blogger already has -- re-reading a published post and checking it by eye for a disclosure. It names no competing product or company. The checker itself makes no network request of any kind: the browser page parses pasted HTML in your own browser, and the CLI reads only local files.

Never written a disclosure yet? See this checker vs. Post Affiliate Pro's Disclosure Generator, or read what disclosure Amazon Associates and the FTC actually require.

Opposite halves of the same problem: Post Affiliate Pro's Disclosure Generator writes new disclosure text from a template, for someone who does not have wording yet. Post Affiliate Pro's Disclosure Generator is a free page that produces new FTC-compliant disclosure text from a template — useful for a blog, YouTube channel, or social account that does not have disclosure wording yet. Post Affiliate Pro itself, of which the generator is one free page, is affiliate-network-management software sold under an ongoing subscription account to merchants running their own affiliate programs. Post Affiliate Pro's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific plan names or pricing, so only its well-documented category and identity are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This checker does the opposite job. It does not write or template any text. what-disclosure-does-amazon-associates-a.text:
← Back to Affiliate Disclosure Checker

What disclosure does Amazon Associates and the FTC actually require?

Two separate obligations sit on top of each other here, and mixing them up is the mistake this page exists to prevent: a general legal standard from the FTC that applies to any affiliate or sponsored content, and a specific contractual term from Amazon that applies only to Amazon Associates links.

The FTC's Endorsement Guides: a general standard

The FTC's position, stated in its Endorsement Guides, is that a material connection between an endorser and a seller — including an affiliate commission — must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously, in plain language, close to the claim it relates to, and before the reader has to act on it (click the link, add the item to a cart). A disclosure that exists only in an about page, a footer, or after several affiliate links have already appeared does not meet that standard for a reader who arrives partway down the page from search.

Amazon's Associates Program Operating Agreement: a specific term

Separately, and in addition to the FTC standard, Amazon's own Associates Program Operating Agreement requires that every page carrying an Associates link include a statement to the effect of:

As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.

This is a contractual requirement with Amazon, not a suggestion, and it is specific wording — a generic "this post contains affiliate links" note satisfies the FTC's general standard but does not satisfy Amazon's own term. Amazon has terminated Associates accounts for missing this statement, which ends the account's entire earning history, not just future commissions on the page in question.

Where to put it

PlacementMeets FTC guidance?Meets Amazon's term?
Near the top of the post, before the first affiliate linkYesYes, if the exact Amazon statement is included
Immediately beside the first affiliate mentionYesYes, if the exact Amazon statement is included
Only in a sitewide footer or About pageNo — not conspicuous to a reader landing mid-pageNo — Amazon's term is per-page, not sitewide
After the affiliate links, at the bottom of a long postNo — too late for a reader who already clickedPresent, but likely too late to be "clear and conspicuous" if ever reviewed

Checking it automatically before you publish

Run the CLI against a built site's output directory as part of your publish step:

node cli.mjs check dist --strict

Exits non-zero if any page has an affiliate link with no disclosure before it, or an Amazon link missing Amazon's own exact statement. It reads only the local files you name — no network call, ever.

Common questions

Are the Amazon rule and the FTC rule the same thing?

No, and meeting one does not automatically meet the other. The FTC's Endorsement Guides are a general legal standard: a clear and conspicuous disclosure, in plain language, before a reader encounters the affiliate link. Amazon's Associates Program Operating Agreement is a specific contractual term with Amazon: it requires that exact statement, on every page carrying an Associates link, regardless of how clearly you have disclosed some other way.

What counts as "before" the link?

FTC guidance treats a disclosure buried at the bottom of a long page, after several affiliate links, as too late — a reader who clicked the first link never saw it. A disclosure near the top of the post, or immediately next to the first affiliate mention, is the safer placement. This tool checks exactly that: whether the earliest disclosure phrase it finds comes before the earliest affiliate link it finds, in the page's own reading order.

Does a footer-only or about-page-only disclosure count?

Not under FTC guidance, and not under this tool's check either — a disclosure that exists somewhere on the site but not on the page with the link is not "clear and conspicuous" to a reader who lands on that page from search or a shared link, which is how most affiliate content is actually read.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report which known affiliate-link and disclosure-phrase patterns appear in a page's text, and their order — nothing more. It is not legal advice, and it is not a determination that any page complies with the FTC's Endorsement Guides or Amazon's Associates Program Operating Agreement. Read the source documents linked above and consult a professional if you need a determination you can rely on.
